title: Fed’s Lisa Cook puts off White House hearing over Trump’s allegations
article:
(Oct 14): Federal Reserve (Fed) governor Lisa Cook says she will be unable to attend a Nov 5 hearing at the White House that’s part of a new investigation into mortgage fraud allegations by US President Donald Trump.

Cook will be “executing her official duties as a governor at financial and monetary policy meetings in Europe” then, her lawyer, Abbe Lowell, said in a letter to the White House on Tuesday.

Lowell wrote that a hearing would have to take place after the Fed’s Dec 8-9 meeting so that Cook had enough time to prepare and to accommodate other scheduling conflicts.

In a memo last week, Trump announced that a committee would investigate his claims that Cook committed mortgage fraud. He said she’d have to appear at the White House for a hearing to defend herself. The investigation is the latest escalation in Trump’s ongoing effort to oust Cook from her role at the Fed.

Trump first attempted to fire Cook last year, the first such action by a president in the Fed’s history. Earlier this year, the Supreme Court held that Trump failed to provide Cook with enough notice and an opportunity to defend herself before attempting to remove her, but didn’t spell out what that procedure should look like.

The justices left it to the White House to create a process that would survive another round of legal wrangling.

See also: US existing-home sales edged up ahead of mortgage-rate shock

Cook has denied the mortgage fraud allegations, casting them as a pretext to remove her from office and allow the president to reshape the Fed more to his liking.

Lowell, in his letter, expressed scepticism about “the objectivity and fitness of the committee for its assigned purpose”.

“For example, one of the committee’s three members,” Trump’s chief economic adviser, Kevin Hassett, “already has publicly insinuated that the president has “cause” to fire Governor Cook,” he said.

See also: US small-business optimism falls on dimmer economic outlook

title: Stocks bounce from lows on Williams’ rate remarks
article:
(Oct 14): Stocks bounced from session lows as speculation the Federal Reserve (Fed) won’t be forced to raise rates aggressively offset lingering worries about elevated oil prices and the outlook for artificial intelligence.

While the S&P 500 closed little changed, most of its firms rose after Fed Bank of New York president John Williams said he still sees one more hike as appropriate this year, but currently doesn’t believe it will be necessary to lift rates again in 2027. Bond yields fell. A sell-off in chipmakers waned, also helping sentiment. Microsoft Corp rose to a record.

“I haven’t changed my view that it may be appropriate to have one more rate hike,” Williams told Bloomberg News. “I don’t think at this time I have any reason to believe that we would need to do more” after that.

His remarks came ahead of a key reading on consumer prices. Higher gasoline costs probably led to quicker overall inflation in September even as underlying price pressures moderated.

“Confirmation that underlying inflation moderated last month would allow the Fed to approach the timing of its next rate hike with patience rather than urgency,” said Ian Lyngen at BMO Capital Markets.

Fed governor Christopher Waller said the surge in long-term Treasury yields is helping to curb demand in rate-sensitive sectors such as housing and automobiles, doing some of the work of tighter monetary policy.

See also: S&P 500 holds firm as banks report earnings, chipmakers slump

“When yields go up, is that going to impact interest-sensitive sectors like housing and autos and other things? Yeah, of course it is,” Waller said at Bloomberg’s New Economy Forum in New Delhi. While that isn’t the Fed’s intention, higher yields are “doing a little bit of the work,” he said.

As the earnings season got underway, JPMorgan Chase & Co, Citigroup Inc and Wells Fargo & Co set a fresh record in the third quarter for how much they earned from lending, with customers continuing to borrow even as interest rates increased.

As Wall Street’s fixed-income desks struggled in the third quarter, their rivals in equities seized a rare opening to outshine their market brethren.

See also: Goldman’s equity traders post big haul as credit, rates miss

Equities divisions at five of the largest US banks are on track to deliver more than US$66 billion of revenue in the first nine months of the year, roughly US$3 billion higher than what’s expected from units handling bonds, currencies and commodities. Part of that was driven by prime brokerage operations catering to hedge funds and other big stock investors.

title: Apple unveils US$299 HomeView Hub as part of new smart home push
article:
(Oct 14): Apple Inc introduced a new device called the HomeView, a US$299 display that serves as the centrepiece of its push to challenge Amazon.com Inc and Alphabet Inc’s Google in the smart home market.

The product, which will be available on Nov 13, relies mainly on hands-free voice commands and uses facial recognition to provide a personalised software experience for each member of the household. There are no physical buttons on the HomeView, though its 7-inch touch screen has a grid of apps that will instantly feel familiar to iPhone and iPad users.

Apple is framing the HomeView as the ideal showcase for its Siri AI assistant: Using a built-in camera, the device can instantly recognise up to six different users and give personalised responses for each individual, whether they’re using it as a cooking companion, videoconferencing with a relative or just listening to music through its speakers.

To help rapidly expand its presence in the smart home, the company is partnering with LG Electronics Inc and Schneider Electric SE to release a lineup of “Apple Home Collection” accessories, such as indoor and outdoor cameras, a video doorbell, thermostats, and door locks. Apple codeveloped the hardware, which will begin shipping in December at prices ranging from US$199 to US$399.

Alongside the HomeView, the company also announced an upgraded Apple TV 4K set-top box — now with built-in microphones and an easier-to-find remote control — and the HomePod mini 2 speaker, which comes in a new batch of colors and has lighting animations that match the album art of whatever song is being played.

See also: ASML’s guidance key to instill confidence in fragile chip trade

Both of those products have increased in cost compared with their predecessors, part of a broader wave of price hikes fuelled by the shortage of memory chips and other components. The US$149 HomePod mini 2 will be available on Oct 30, and the US$299 Apple TV 4K will follow on Nov 13. That compares with a starting price of US$199 for the previous TV box and US$129 for the HomePod mini. Both new devices can be pre-ordered on Tuesday, along with the HomeView.

Apple is offering two different styles of its first-ever smart display. The one most consumers will purchase is a tabletop design with an aluminum base and an adjustable stainless steel hinge that lets users freely tilt the display on counters or nightstands.

See also: China’s CXMT claims memory advances ahead of Samsung, Hynix

The company will also sell another version of the HomeView, at the same US$299 price, that’s designed to be placed on the wall. The tabletop version is powered with a standard USB-C cable, while the wall-mounted product will support a range of different options, including power over Ethernet, or PoE, which could ease installation.

The 7-inch screen is square in shape — a design Apple chose to help distinguish it from the wider displays of TVs and monitors — and automatically adjusts its brightness and colour balance to match the HomeView’s environment. The screen has a maximum brightness of 500 nits and can dial all the way down to 0.3 nits, the lowest level of any display the company has ever manufactured. That will prevent it from being a distraction at night on a bedside table.

The software experience is identical across both models, with the ability to show various clock-like “faces” whenever HomeView is idle. There’s a Photos Face, an Apple Watch-like Modular Face with four customisable widgets, a Snoopy Face with playful animations of the Peanuts comic character, and several more traditional clock faces.

Some faces, like one called Flow, can shift colours and patterns based on movement detected in front of the device’s 12-megapixel Center Stage camera. Alternatively, users can choose to have HomeView serve as a smart home command centre, showing controls for door locks, lights and other gadgets, or provide a live feed of connected video cameras.

Whenever HomeView recognises household members, it will display their personalised home screen of applications, widgets and calendar appointments. Siri AI, Apple’s recently upgraded digital assistant, is able to leverage its database of knowledge about each specific user when answering requests or sending messages. The HomeView always relies on a nearby iPhone for personal context; that data isn’t stored directly on the device.

Apple has adopted several privacy safeguards to prevent one family member from seeing another’s private data. If a known user leaves the camera’s view, HomeView will revert to its default shared household mode in just a few seconds. Additionally, each person’s iPhone must be on the same WiFi network as the HomeView in order for Siri AI to tap into personal data. The phone also must have recently been unlocked.

To stay ahead of Singapore and the region’s corporate and economic trends, click here for Latest Section

Apple said it wants HomeView to be useful when someone first wakes up in the morning — without requiring them to authenticate — so this “recent” window stretches several hours, and the company may further adjust it based on customer feedback.

If HomeView can’t identify who’s standing in front of it, the device will show a generic screen with less extensive smart home controls: Guests can adjust a thermostat or toggle lights, but they’re unable to control smart locks or access a security camera’s video history, for example.

HomeView includes versions of the company’s popular apps, like Apple TV, Music, Calendar, Podcasts, Safari and more, but there’s no App Store on the device. According to the company, third-party audio and video software that supports Apple’s CarPlay architecture will appear on the smart display just as they would on a vehicle dashboard. This will let services like Spotify work on the HomeView even without a conventional app marketplace.

By bringing an iPhone close to the HomeView, you can “hand off” music playback, FaceTime video calls and Safari web browsing sessions to the new device. Apple has also created a special cooking mode that converts recipes into step-by-step guides optimised for the screen. Whenever a cooking time is mentioned, you can simply tap it to create a timer for the specified length.

In a hands-on demonstration, the HomeView’s speakers were loud and clear — though the bass wasn’t as impactful as on the full-sized HomePod speaker, which costs US$349. The new device is smaller than many people might expect, and the HomeView’s display is shorter than an iPhone 17 Pro Max. Apple’s demonstrations of Siri worked smoothly when asking general knowledge questions and in specific scenarios like asking about appointments and controlling lights.

But the biggest challenge for the HomeView is whether it will prove reliable and work consistently as the central element in complex smart home environments. As a blend of the iPad, Apple Watch and HomePod, the appeal and functionality is there: Apple just needs to prove that the dependability will be just as impressive.

The various devices that Apple developed with LG and Schneider Electric include:

These products, known as the Apple Home Collection, will start shipping in December. Availability will be limited to Apple’s own stores before expanding to other retailers in the coming months. All of the gadgets can be set up using an iPhone without requiring any extra apps or separate accounts, and they integrate seamlessly into Apple’s ecosystem.

The latest Apple TV 4K now has microphones built into the set-top box itself. That allows for hands-free Siri AI voice commands from your couch, even when the remote is out of reach. On the TV screen, Apple’s assistant replies with text overlays rather than speaking aloud. But it will be useful for asking to play a TV episode or show that a friend recommended when the actual name escapes you.

The aluminium remote’s design is unchanged, but it can now emit a sound when lost in the cushions to make it easier to find. Users can even activate precision finding on an iPhone to pinpoint the remote’s exact location if needed.

Apple is giving the new box one other exclusive feature: You can group up to four HomePods for immersive front and rear surround sound. Previously, they could only serve as front speakers. But now you can combine pairs of the second-generation HomePod and the HomePod mini 2 — or four of the same speaker — for a much more engrossing audio experience.

Even with its newfound functionality, the Apple TV 4K’s increasingly steep price might dissuade all but the most hardcore home theater enthusiasts from upgrading.

Apple’s small wired speaker, now US$20 more expensive, looks identical to its predecessor save for fresh colours. The new choices include green, pink and blue, along with more neutral white and midnight options. The chipset inside has been upgraded to the S10 for faster processing, and a new “Sound Glow” feature makes the touch surface on top illuminate in different hues. It can show the same color palette as album artwork or match ambient soundscapes like rain or forest sounds.

And for recent Macs with WiFi 6E, the HomePod mini 2 can be used as a default external speaker with low-latency audio when playing games or joining video calls.

Siri AI will eventually come to the device, but not until a “later” software update, according to Apple.

The company is unveiling this wave of smart home hardware just days before the arrival of its long-awaited iPhone Duo foldable phone. Consumers can place orders for that device on Oct 16, a week before it hits stores.

Apple is also planning to unveil a touch-screen MacBook Pro and an updated iPad mini — both with sharper OLED screens — at the end of this month, Bloomberg News has reported. It’s all part of a record-setting surge of new products under chief executive officer John Ternus, who took the helm last month.

title: How to Invest in Japanese Small-Cap Stocks from Singapore
article:
This article is for educational purposes only and does not constitute financial advice or a recommendation to buy or sell any security. Investors should consider their objectives, financial situation and risk tolerance before investing.
Buying Toyota or Sony from Singapore is straightforward. Finding and buying a lesser-known Japanese small cap takes a little more homework.
Japan has a deep pool of listed companies across manufacturing, technology, healthcare, and consumer industries. Many are less familiar to international investors.
Access is no longer the difficult part. The bigger questions are how much capital you need, what trading costs to expect and whether you are comfortable researching companies that may receive far less coverage than Japan’s large caps.
Start With a Broker That Offers Japan Market Access
The first step is finding a brokerage that supports direct trading on the Tokyo Stock Exchange (TSE).
Platforms available in Singapore include
Interactive Brokers
,
POEMS
, and
Moomoo Singapore
.
Once Japanese equities are enabled, the process is familiar: fund the account, convert Singapore dollars into yen if needed, search for the company using its four-digit stock code, and place an order.
Brokerage commission is only part of the cost. FX spreads, minimum commissions, and custody or market-data fees can matter, especially on smaller trades.
Japan’s 100-Share Trading Unit Can Affect Position Sizing
One feature that can catch first-time investors out is Japan’s standard trading unit.
Domestic TSE-listed shares generally trade in
lots of 100
.
A stock priced at ¥2,000 therefore requires about:
¥2,000 × 100 shares = ¥200,000
At ¥5,000 a share, one standard lot would cost ¥500,000.
That can make position sizing awkward for smaller portfolios. A company may have a relatively small market capitalisation but still require a meaningful upfront investment because of its share price.
Some platforms may allow smaller positions, but investors should check whether they are buying regular TSE-listed shares, fractional shares, or another product.
Prime, Standard and Growth Are Not Size Labels
The TSE is divided into
Prime, Standard, and Growth markets
, but those segments should not be treated as shorthand for company size.
Prime contains many of Japan’s largest businesses, Standard covers established companies across a range of sizes, while Growth is aimed at businesses with higher growth potential and generally higher risk.
A Growth listing is not automatically a small cap. Neither is a Standard company necessarily mature or slow-growing.
SmallCap Asia’s earlier guide to the
Tokyo Stock Exchange
goes into the market structure in more detail.
For investors looking specifically at smaller companies, market capitalisation, liquidity, and business fundamentals matter more than the segment name.
Trading From Singapore Is Relatively Convenient
Japan is only one hour ahead of Singapore.
The
TSE trades from 9:00 a.m. to 11:30 a.m. and 12:30 p.m. to 3:30 p.m.
Japan time. That works out to 8:00 a.m. to 10:30 a.m. and 11:30 a.m. to 2:30 p.m. in Singapore.
That makes Japanese stocks considerably easier to follow during the day than US markets. The bigger issue for small-cap investors is liquidity.
Some smaller Japanese companies may trade relatively few shares each day, which can lead to wider bid-ask spreads and bigger price moves when larger orders enter the market.
Checking trading volume before buying matters. Using a limit order can also give investors more control over the price they pay.
The Yen Can Change Your Return
Buying Japanese shares means taking on currency exposure as well.
A stock may rise in yen terms but deliver a weaker return once converted back into Singapore dollars if the yen falls against SGD. A stronger yen can boost SGD returns.
There is also the cost of converting currencies in the first place. Brokers use different FX pricing models, so frequent conversions can eat into returns even when trading commissions look low.
The aim does not have to be predicting where SGD/JPY goes next.
It is simply recognising that the company is only one part of the return. The currency matters too.
Dividends May Arrive Lower Than the Headline Figure
For Singapore-resident individuals,
foreign dividends received in Singapore are generally not taxable
, subject to limited exceptions.
Japan may still deduct withholding tax before the dividend reaches your account. Under the
Singapore–Japan Avoidance of Double Taxation Agreement
, withholding tax on dividends is generally capped at 15% of the gross amount for individual investors who qualify for treaty benefits.
As those dividends are generally not taxable in Singapore, there is usually no Singapore tax liability against which to claim a foreign tax credit.
Investors should still check how their broker applies treaty rates and whether documentation is required.
Research Is Where Japanese Small Caps Get Harder
Buying the shares is relatively simple. Researching the company can be less so.
Smaller Japanese businesses may have limited analyst coverage, lower trading volumes and fewer English-language investor materials than household names such as Toyota or Sony.
That makes primary sources more important. Check the latest financial results, annual reports and exchange announcements, along with cash flow, debt and management’s capital-allocation record.
Language can be another hurdle. English disclosure has improved, but the depth of translated material still varies between companies.
Japan’s corporate-governance reforms have also put greater focus on capital efficiency and shareholder returns. That may create opportunities, but investors should judge changes company by company rather than assume every small cap will benefit.
What to Check Before Buying Your First Japanese Small Cap
Before placing an order, check:
whether your broker offers direct TSE access
the total cost after commissions and FX
whether the 100-share trading unit fits your portfolio
how liquid the stock is
whether enough information is available to understand the business
how yen movements could affect your return
Buying the shares is straightforward. The real work is deciding which smaller Japanese companies are worth owning and whether the extra research, currency exposure, and liquidity risk are justified.
